newsitem.title: USA: U.S. manufacturing booms in March, housing eases.
newsitem.headline: U.S. manufacturing booms in March, housing eases.

text.p: A manufacturing boom pushed factories to their steepest operating levels in two years during March, the Federal Reserve said on Wednesday, reviving fears of more interest-rate rises as early as next month.

Separately, the Commerce Department said builders broke ground on fewer new homes and apartments last month than in February but still finished the first quarter with a higher total than in the final three months of last year.

Analysts said a potential leveling off in the housing sector was not enough by itself to prevent the central bank from again raising interest rates as early as May 20 in the face of strained factory operating levels to meet vibrant consumer demand.
Total output by the nation's mines, factories and utilities climbed a stronger-than-expected 0.9 percent last month following a revised 0.6 percent February pickup.

The capacity use rate, which measures how near to production limits businesses are operating, jumped to 84.1 percent from a revised 83.6 percent in February -- the highest rate since 84.3 percent in March 1995.

"We've certainly moved into an inflationary danger zone," said economist Anthony Chan of Banc One Investment Advisors Corp. in Columbus, Ohio. An operating rate above 84 percent signals rising potential for bottlenecks from higher prices for raw materials and bigger wage demands from employees, Chan added.

In its report, the Commerce Department said construction starts on new homes and apartments fell 6.4 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.43 million after a revised 10.7 percent jump in February, when unseasonabvly mild weather boosted building activity.
Costlier mortgage rates, which topped 8 percent in April for a 30-year loan and are predicted to stay there for the rest of the year, are expected to tamp down housing activity.

Members of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee decided on March 25 to boost short-term interest rates a quarter percentage point, citing the risk that strong demand could fire up inflation. The FOMC next meets on May 20.

Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago, said manufacturing industries clearly were responding in March to strong demand for new cars, computers and other goods and that will keep the Fed on edge.

"We now have a very stretched economy -- employment is high, GDP vs. potential growth is high and now we have a capacity use rate that is so high that some firms will be testing their ability to raise prices," Dederick said.
"The economy is clearly growing too fast for the Fed's comfort," he added, so the question is not whether the central bank will raise rates, "but how far and how fast."
After expanding at a 3.8 percent annual rate in last year's fourth quarter, gross domestic product is widely predicted to have exceeded 4 percent in the first three months this year.

The Federal Reserve has said it considers growth in the 2 percent to 2-1/4 percent range sustainable without igniting inflation that could cripple an expansion now in its seventh year after the last recession in 1990-91.

The Fed said growth in U.S. industrial output accelerated to an annual rate of 5.6 percent in the first quarter this year, up from 4.5 percent in the final three months of last year, when strikes in the auto industry put a damper on output.

Total manufacturing production jumped 0.9 percent in both February and March this year, driven primarily by more demand for costly and long-lasting durable goodss like household appliances and computers.
Production by mining industries was up 0.9 percent in March after a strong 1.5 percent gain in February, while utilities boosted output by 0.8 percent following a 3.4 percent decline in February.
The drop in March homebuilding was concentrated in the Midwest, where heavy rains and flooding pulled construction activity down at the steepest rate in more than three years.
Starts plunged 20.2 percent in the Midwest during March to a rate of 292,000 -- the biggest monthly decline since a 25.8 percent drop in March 1994, the department said.
But Midwestern housing starts had shot up 40.8 percent in February.
Starts also fell during March in the South, the nation's biggest regional housing market, by 7.1 percent to an annual rate of 619,000 after a 13.1 percent increase in February.

March starts increased 11.5 percent in the Northeast to a rate of 146,000 after a 28 percent fall in February. In the West, March starts rose 2.5 percent to 368,000 a year after a 4.4 percent increase in February.
